newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Brierley says to defend ASC proceedings.
newsitem.headline: Brierley says to defend ASC proceedings.

text.p: New Zealand's Brierley Investments Ltd said on Friday it will vigorously defend proceedings brought by Australia's corporate watchdog over trading in the shares of newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.

Earlier on Friday, the Australian Securities Commission (ASC) said it applied to the Corporations and Securities Panel for a declaration that trading in Fairfax shares by Merrill Lynch and Brierley was unacceptable conduct.
Brierley said the ASC statement that it had entered into swap agreements in respect of about 4.9 percent of Fairfax shares was misleading.
The ASC omitted to state that the transactions did not require Brierley's counter-party to acquire, hold or dispose of any Fairfax shares at any time, Brierley said.
"The agreements referred to are purely economic, synthetic financial transactions," it said.
"At no time do these arrangements give BIL any right or entitlements to any Fairfax shares," it said.
Brierley said it was entirely open and appropriate for corporates to seek synthetic cover in the normal course of business.
These synthetic transactions are quite common and it was unfortunate the ASC had not provided specific guidelines to the market about their use, Brierley said.
It also said its first knowledge of the ASC action came when the ASC issued a press release on Friday afternoon and that at no time had the ASC approached it to discuss the allegation.
"BIL finds the ASC's conduct in this regard, extraordinary," it said.
As a consequence Brierley was unable to rely on the three percent creep rule in the Corporations Law to acquire further Fairfax shares until six months after December 31, 1996.

In its press release, the ASC said: "An investigation by the ASC has revealed that Merrill Lynch (Australia) Futures Ltd and a subsidiary of BIL entered swap arrangements in respect of approximately 4.9 percent of Fairfax shares in March 1997."
ASC said a parcel of about 4.9 percent of Fairfax shares had been acquired by an entity in the Merrill Lynch group in January 1997.
Merrill Lynch sold about 22.5 million Fairfax shares or about three percent of the media group's issued capital on June over three days, June 17, 24 and 27, the ASC said.
Between June 17 and July 4, a subsidiary or susidiaries of Brierley purchased about the same number of Fairfax share through the Australian Stock Exchange, the ASC said.
Brierley became Fairfax's biggest single shareholder when it acquired 19.9 percent of the company on December 16, 1996, from Canadian publisher Conrad Black, who had held about 25 percent.
In February, Fairfax shareholders rejected a proposal that Brierley be permitted to purchase a further 4.9 percent of the newspaper publisher formerly held by Black, the ASC said.
As a consequence Brierley was unable to rely on the three percent creep rule in the Corporations Law to acquire further Fairfax shares until six months after December 31, 1996, the ASC said.
Fairfax shares closed three cents up at A$3.19.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
